detail.en: Follow the words as it plays

text.en: Find the notes of line 1: each one waits until you're on it.

The old sea captain W. B. Whall wrote that the whole crew sang it together at a quick march, as they walked away with the rope. When crews got smaller and could no longer walk away with anything, the song dropped out of use.

source.en: W. B. Whall, Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties (3rd ed., 1913), p. 107, Internet Archive

text.en: Hear line 1, then sing it back.
Hear line 2, then sing it back.
Now lines 1 and 2 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 3, then sing it back.
Hear line 4, then sing it back.
Now lines 3 and 4 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 5, then sing it back.
Hear line 6, then sing it back.
Now lines 5 and 6 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 7, then sing it back.
Hear line 8, then sing it back.
Now lines 7 and 8 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Verse 1 start to end, with the guide.
Chorus start to end, with the guide.
The whole song, with the guide.
Sing your part with the other parts, and the guide with you. Hold your line while the others move.
The guide drops out: your part with the others only. Give me my note plays your first note quietly.
Once more on your own, from the top.
Record the tune of Drunken Sailor in Sing, with the other parts playing.
Richard Terry, who printed this tune in 1921, named it as one of the shanties in the old modes, rather than in a modern major or minor key.

source.en: R. R. Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I (1921), introduction, Internet Archive
